scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

If she’s not willing to contribute, she shouldn’t expect you to do all the work. - Your dad, who *does* cook and handle chores, is often left to pick up the slack because your mom refuses to participate. This is a systemic issue in your household. 2. **Your Circumstances vs. Her Expectations:** - You’re in high school with online classes, which means you have a lot of work to do. Expecting you to cook dinner *every night* while managing schoolwork is unreasonable. Your mom’s expectation ignores the fact that you’re not just "home all day"—you’re also responsible for your education. - She dismissed your workload by saying, *"It doesn’t take that long to cook."* That’s a dismissive and unfair statement, especially when she herself doesn’t cook and expects others to do it for her. 3. **Her Reaction Was Unjustified:** - She screamed at you and called you "useless" for not cooking. This was emotionally abusive and unfair. Her anger was directed at you, not at the real issue: *her own lack of contribution*. - If she’s ashamed of the family, it’s because she’s not holding up her end of the responsibilities—not because you’re failing to cook. 4. **Your Mom’s Poor Cooking Skills:** - You mentioned she doesn’t even *try* to learn. This is a red flag. If she can’t or won’t cook, she shouldn’t expect others to do it for her. Your dad’s efforts to teach her were ignored, and now he’s left to cook late at night or skip meals entirely. - Your dad’s role as the primary cook and chore-doer is unsustainable. This is a gendered imbalance that needs to be addressed. 5. **Your Right to Say No:** - You *were not* in the wrong for refusing to cook. You had valid reasons: - You have schoolwork. - Your mom doesn’t cook either. - Your dad is already overburdened. - Pushing back against unfair expectations is healthy, especially when it comes to household labor. 6. **The Broader Issue: Gender Roles & Fairness:** - This situation highlights an unfair dynamic where women (especially mothers) are often expected to handle cooking and childcare without reciprocity. Your mom’s refusal to contribute while expecting you to do all the work is a classic example of this imbalance. - Your dad’s role as the primary cook and chore-doer is unsustainable and unfair. This is a systemic issue that needs to be addressed, not just with you but with your mom. ### **Was It Right or Wrong?** **You were absolutely right to refuse.** - Your mom’s expectations were unreasonable, unfair, and ignored the reality of your situation (schoolwork, her own lack of contribution, and your dad’s overwork). - Her reaction was abusive and unjustified. She should have taken responsibility for her own actions instead of blaming you. - You’re not responsible for fixing a broken system where your mom refuses to help and your dad is overburdened. ### **What Should Happen Now?** 1. **Have a Calm Conversation with Your Mom:** - Tell her that you’re not going to cook every night because: - You have schoolwork. - She doesn’t cook either. - Your dad is already doing too much. - Ask her to contribute more—whether that’s cooking, helping with chores, or at least not expecting you to do everything. 2. **Encourage Your Dad to Set Boundaries:** - Your dad should not be the only one cooking or doing chores. This is unsustainable and unfair to him. - If he’s already cooking late or skipping meals, he should speak up and demand fairness. 3. **Address the Emotional Fallout:** - Your mom’s reaction was hurtful. You deserve respect, and she should apologize for her behavior. - If she continues to blame you or refuse to change, consider involving a family mediator or therapist to help address these dynamics. 4. **Protect Your Mental Health:** - If this situation continues to cause stress, it’s okay to prioritize your well-being. You’re not obligated to fix a broken household dynamic alone. - If your mom continues to be abusive or unreasonable, consider discussing this with a trusted adult (like a school counselor or family friend) for support. ### **Final Verdict:** **You were 100% right to refuse.** This isn’t about being "lazy" or "ungrateful"—it’s about fairness, respect, and recognizing that household labor should be shared equitably. Your mom’s expectations were unreasonable, and her reaction was unfair. You deserve better, and so does your dad. Would you like help brainstorming how to approach this conversation with your mom? You’re not alone in this.
